problems.title: Constant-pressure expansion work
problems.scenario:
A piston–cylinder device holds gas at a constant pressure of **200 kPa**. The gas is heated and its volume rises from $V_1 = 0.10\ \text{m}^3$ to $V_2 = 0.30\ \text{m}^3$.

How much **boundary work** does the gas do?
hints: The pressure is constant, so you don't need to integrate — there's a one-line formula for boundary work at constant pressure.
$W_b = P\,(V_2 - V_1)$. Watch the units: $\text{kPa}\cdot\text{m}^3 = \text{kJ}$.
problems.solution:
For a **constant-pressure** process the boundary work is the rectangle under the path on a $P$-$V$ diagram:

$$W_b = P\,(V_2 - V_1)$$

Substitute the numbers:

$$W_b = 200\ \text{kPa} \times (0.30 - 0.10)\ \text{m}^3 = 200 \times 0.20 = 40\ \text{kJ}$$

The result is **positive**, so the gas does work *on* the piston as it expands. Unit check: $\text{kPa}\cdot\text{m}^3 = \text{kJ}$. ✓

problems.title: Heating gas in a rigid tank
problems.scenario:
**2 kg** of air sits in a **rigid, sealed tank**. It is heated from $T_1 = 300\ \text{K}$ to $T_2 = 400\ \text{K}$.

How much heat is added? Take $c_v = 0.718\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.
hints: "Rigid" is the key word — what does that tell you about the boundary work?
With $W_b = 0$, the energy balance $Q - W = \Delta U$ collapses to $Q = \Delta U$.
For an ideal gas, $\Delta U = m\,c_v\,\Delta T$.
problems.solution:
A **rigid** tank means the volume can't change, so the boundary work is zero:

$$W_b = 0$$

The closed-system energy balance $Q - W = \Delta U$ then reduces to

$$Q = \Delta U = m\,c_v\,\Delta T$$

Substitute:

$$Q = 2\ \text{kg} \times 0.718\ \tfrac{\text{kJ}}{\text{kg·K}} \times (400 - 300)\ \text{K} = 143.6\ \text{kJ}$$

All of the heat goes into raising the internal energy because no work leaves the system.

problems.title: Constant-pressure heating of air
problems.scenario:
**1.5 kg** of air in a piston–cylinder is heated at **constant pressure** from $T_1 = 300\ \text{K}$ to $T_2 = 500\ \text{K}$.

Find the **heat added**. Take $c_p = 1.005\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.
hints: There's both heat *and* boundary work here, so $Q = \Delta U$ would be wrong. Is there a shortcut for constant pressure?
For a constant-pressure process with only boundary work, the $W_b$ and $PV$ terms combine: $Q = \Delta H$.
$\Delta H = m\,c_p\,\Delta T$ for an ideal gas.
problems.solution:
At **constant pressure** with only boundary work, the energy balance simplifies neatly. Starting from $Q - W_b = \Delta U$ and using $W_b = P\,\Delta V$:

$$Q = \Delta U + P\,\Delta V = \Delta(U + PV) = \Delta H$$

So you can skip computing the work separately and use enthalpy directly:

$$Q = \Delta H = m\,c_p\,\Delta T = 1.5 \times 1.005 \times (500 - 300) = 301.5\ \text{kJ}$$

This is why $c_p$ (not $c_v$) is the right specific heat for a constant-pressure process.

problems.title: Isothermal expansion of an ideal gas
problems.scenario:
**0.5 kg** of air at a constant **300 K** expands in a piston–cylinder from $P_1 = 600\ \text{kPa}$ to $P_2 = 100\ \text{kPa}$.

Find the **boundary work** done by the gas. Take $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.
hints: For an ideal gas at constant temperature, $PV = \text{const}$, so the work integral gives a logarithm.
$W_b = mRT\ln(V_2/V_1)$, and since $T$ is constant, $V_2/V_1 = P_1/P_2$.
So $W_b = mRT\ln(P_1/P_2)$.
problems.solution:
For an **isothermal** expansion of an ideal gas, $PV = mRT = \text{const}$, and the boundary work integrates to a log:

$$W_b = mRT\ln\frac{V_2}{V_1}$$

Because $T$ is constant, $V_2/V_1 = P_1/P_2$, so we can use the (given) pressures directly:

$$W_b = mRT\ln\frac{P_1}{P_2} = 0.5 \times 0.287 \times 300 \times \ln\frac{600}{100}$$

$$W_b = 43.05 \times \ln 6 = 43.05 \times 1.792 = 77.1\ \text{kJ}$$

Note: for an isothermal ideal-gas process $\Delta U = 0$, so the first law gives $Q = W_b = 77.1\ \text{kJ}$ — all the heat added leaves as work.

problems.title: Boiling water at constant pressure
problems.scenario:
**2 kg** of saturated *liquid* water in a piston–cylinder at a constant **300 kPa** is heated until it becomes saturated *vapor*.

Using $h_{fg} = 2163.5\ \text{kJ/kg}$ at 300 kPa, find the **heat added**.
hints: This is a constant-pressure process, so the constant-pressure shortcut applies again.
$Q = \Delta H = m\,(h_2 - h_1)$. Going from saturated liquid to saturated vapor, $h_2 - h_1 = h_{fg}$.
So $Q = m\,h_{fg}$.
problems.solution:
Phase change happens at **constant pressure** (and temperature), so once again $Q = \Delta H$. Going from saturated liquid ($h_f$) to saturated vapor ($h_g$), the enthalpy change per unit mass is exactly the latent heat of vaporization:

$$h_2 - h_1 = h_g - h_f = h_{fg}$$

Therefore:

$$Q = m\,h_{fg} = 2\ \text{kg} \times 2163.5\ \tfrac{\text{kJ}}{\text{kg}} = 4327\ \text{kJ}$$

The temperature stays fixed at $T_{sat}$ during the whole process; all the heat goes into the phase change, not into raising temperature.

problems.title: Polytropic compression work
problems.scenario:
Air in a piston–cylinder is compressed in a **polytropic** process $PV^{1.3} = \text{const}$ from state 1 ($P_1 = 100\ \text{kPa}$, $V_1 = 0.20\ \text{m}^3$) to a final pressure $P_2 = 600\ \text{kPa}$.

Find the **boundary work** $W_b$. Report the sign (negative = work done *on* the gas).
hints: First you need $V_2$. Rearrange the polytropic relation $P_1V_1^n = P_2V_2^n$ for $V_2$.
Then use $W_b = (P_2V_2 - P_1V_1)/(1-n)$ with $n = 1.3$.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — find $V_2$** by rearranging the polytropic relation $P_1V_1^n = P_2V_2^n$:

$$V_2 = V_1\left(\frac{P_1}{P_2}\right)^{1/n} = 0.20\left(\frac{100}{600}\right)^{1/1.3} = 0.20 \times (0.1667)^{0.769} = 0.0504\ \text{m}^3$$

**Step 2 — apply the polytropic work formula** (valid for $n \neq 1$):

$$W_b = \frac{P_2V_2 - P_1V_1}{1 - n} = \frac{(600)(0.0504) - (100)(0.20)}{1 - 1.3}$$

$$W_b = \frac{30.24 - 20.0}{-0.3} = \frac{10.24}{-0.3} = -34.1\ \text{kJ}$$

The **negative** sign means work is done *on* the gas — exactly what you expect for a compression.

problems.title: Polytropic compression — full first law
problems.scenario:
**0.3 kg** of air is compressed polytropically ($PV^{1.3} = \text{const}$) from $P_1 = 100\ \text{kPa}$, $T_1 = 300\ \text{K}$ to $P_2 = 500\ \text{kPa}$.

Find the **heat transfer** $Q$ and state its direction. Take $c_v = 0.718$ and $R = 0.287\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.
hints: Three steps: find $T_2$, then $W_b$, then close the energy balance $Q = \Delta U + W_b$.
$W_b = mR(T_2 - T_1)/(1-n)$ for an ideal gas; then $\Delta U = m\,c_v\,\Delta T$ and $Q = \Delta U + W_b$.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 — exit temperature** from the polytropic $T$-$P$ relation:

$$T_2 = T_1\left(\frac{P_2}{P_1}\right)^{(n-1)/n} = 300\,(5)^{0.3/1.3} = 300 \times 1.450 = 434.9\ \text{K}$$

**Step 2 — boundary work**, using the ideal-gas form $W_b = mR(T_2-T_1)/(1-n)$:

$$W_b = \frac{0.3 \times 0.287 \times (434.9 - 300)}{1 - 1.3} = \frac{11.62}{-0.3} = -38.7\ \text{kJ}$$

**Step 3 — internal-energy change:**

$$\Delta U = m\,c_v\,\Delta T = 0.3 \times 0.718 \times 134.9 = 29.1\ \text{kJ}$$

**Step 4 — close the energy balance** $Q - W = \Delta U \Rightarrow Q = \Delta U + W_b$:

$$Q = 29.1 + (-38.7) = -9.7\ \text{kJ}$$

The negative result means **heat is rejected** from the gas during the compression.

problems.title: Quenching an aluminum block (calorimetry)
problems.scenario:
A **2 kg** aluminum block at **200 °C** is dropped into **10 kg** of water at **20 °C** in an **insulated** container. Find the **equilibrium temperature**.

Take $c_{\text{Al}} = 0.902$ and $c_{\text{water}} = 4.18\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$.
hints: Insulated + rigid → no heat or work crosses the outer boundary, so the total energy change is zero: heat lost by aluminum = heat gained by water.
For incompressible substances, $\Delta U = m\,c\,\Delta T$. Set $m_{Al}c_{Al}(T_2 - 200) + m_w c_w (T_2 - 20) = 0$.
Solve the linear equation for the single unknown $T_2$.
problems.solution:
The container is insulated and rigid, so $Q = 0$ and $W = 0$; the combined internal energy is conserved. Heat lost by the aluminum equals heat gained by the water:

$$m_{\text{Al}}\,c_{\text{Al}}\,(T_2 - 200) + m_w\,c_w\,(T_2 - 20) = 0$$

This uses the **incompressible** relation $\Delta U = m\,c\,\Delta T$ for each substance. Plug in:

$$2(0.902)(T_2 - 200) + 10(4.18)(T_2 - 20) = 0$$

$$1.804\,T_2 - 360.8 + 41.8\,T_2 - 836 = 0$$

$$43.604\,T_2 = 1196.8 \quad\Rightarrow\quad T_2 = 27.4\ \text{°C}$$

The water's large mass *and* high specific heat keep the final temperature close to its starting value. (Since only temperature **differences** appear, working in °C is fine here.)

problems.title: Two-step heating then expansion
problems.scenario:
**0.8 kg** of air ($c_v = 0.718$, $c_p = 1.005\ \text{kJ/(kg·K)}$) in a piston–cylinder undergoes two steps: (1) **constant-volume** heating from 300 K to 450 K, then (2) **constant-pressure** expansion until the volume **doubles**.

Find the **total heat input**, in kJ.
hints: Treat each step separately. Step 1 is rigid → $Q_1 = \Delta U = m c_v \Delta T$.
Step 2 is constant pressure → $Q_2 = \Delta H = m c_p \Delta T$. First find $T_3$: at constant $P$, doubling $V$ doubles the absolute temperature.
problems.solution:
**Step 1 (constant volume), 300 → 450 K:**

$$Q_1 = m c_v \Delta T = 0.8 \times 0.718 \times 150 = 86.2\ \text{kJ}$$

**Step 2 (constant pressure):** doubling the volume at constant pressure doubles the absolute temperature, so $T_3 = 2 \times 450 = 900$ K, and

$$Q_2 = m c_p \Delta T = 0.8 \times 1.005 \times (900 - 450) = 361.8\ \text{kJ}$$

**Total:**

$$Q = Q_1 + Q_2 = 86.2 + 361.8 = 448\ \text{kJ}$$

Using $c_v$ for the rigid step and $c_p$ for the constant-pressure step is the key decision.
